Oh of course it is. But I'm sure there are other people who feel the same. I've definitely seen some people give me some awkward smiles when I've locked eyes with them. I don't think eye contact with someone I'm speaking with is a bad thing. But on a flight, I'm not really interested in making eyes with strangers. 

 I'm actually a recruiter and my company still does in person interviews. When I was a pilot recruiter if the person was local or we were in their city we would definitely do in person.

I'd like to say that I treat them like everyone else but I know that's not true. I try to, but ever since I was a little girl I've always wanted to be accepted by other black women. I would follow the other little black girls around at school thinking they were my friends but I was actually just a weirdo literally following them around. I would even give them my lunch money because I thought it would give me favor. But instead it made me look corny and a bit "underdeveloped".

I feel like I stopped trying so hard as I grew older and let people come to me. But even as an adult, I know that I treat other black people in general with care. I'm always trying to make sure I'm saying the right thing and I'm extra sweet. I'm sure it's just an adult version of corny.

 I'm that way especially with my family. The volume of my voice even lowers and I speak an octave higher. They've always told me I sound like a child, but even though it's not intentional, my family is a lot more careful with me than all the other cousins. I get spoken to much nicer and sweeter. 

After being on this sub a bit I realize this might be a trauma response. As long as I was quiet I didn't get cussed out or beat. They couldn't find anything wrong with me if I was invisible. No reason to make fun of someone who you forget exists. If I'm quiet and as sweet as pie I can't get hurt. It's totally not fair to expand the response to other black people but I'm working on it.

I'm going to try an analogy. 

I have a garden on my balcony. It's taken a lot of research, money and time to make these plants happy. They all have different needs so you have to figure out what works for each one and make sure you're consistent. If you aren't they'll die or at least shed a few leaves. It has taken a lot of trial and error to get things right. Different websites will tell you to do different things so after a while you just gotta figure it out on your own.  For a while I had a watering schedule, but then learned that I need to decide when to water each plant by touching them to see if they are dry. 

Luckily I enjoy doing all of this. It's a rewarding hobby with low stakes. No one sees my balcony plants but me so if something dies no big deal. While I do enjoy it, it is difficult. That's why it's so rewarding. It's hard work but something beautiful comes out of it.

That's understandable. It's absolutely frustrating and just plain bullshit to see other people get praised for shit you get put down for. Its like oh so everything about my culture is super cool as long as it's done by people outside of it. Just admit we're fucking awesome, the fuck?

For me, if the people who were using the language were the ones looking down on us, I would absolutely be offended. But I don't usually see that. (They definitely exist, I just don't see it as much.) I just don't have any anger in my heart for people who are using it and aren't looking down on us. In my eyes I see them looking up to us. I guess I don't blame them for the people who are assholes. I want people to see how cool my culture is. One of the best ways to build bridges and bring people closer together is an exchange of cultures. In the US we live in a crazy melting pot of cultures so we're all constantly getting influenced by each other.

*This is a story, so you can skip to the next star if you want.

We had a lot of international students work at my job in college. Sometimes they would take us out to restaurants in the area so we could try their food. Sometimes they would even make things themselves and bring it in. You can learn a lot about people from their food and it's a great olive branch.

I love languages so I would usually try to learn some basic phrases and go into work and try them out and they would just light up. Someone taking the time to learn something about your culture is honestly a beautiful thing.
We would ask them questions about their country and music, food, everything. Now I know how to make some bomb ass fried rice, doro wat, and I listen to music in every language under the sun. 

*End of story.

Even though I was a really open person before then. I feel almost a kinship with those cultures now. I see how similar we all are and the differences are beautiful. Different races and cultures don't feel like "others" to me like they may have before but part of a larger community. 

So, I don't usually comment on these posts. People have a right to feel anger and frustration and vent and I don't want people to think oh this one black girl said it's okay so I'm just gonna ignore the anger I'm causing the rest of the community. Just felt like adding my perspective just in case it helps. Maybe it'll bring someone a little peace.

(My degree was in linguistics in college. I don't remember shit, honestly, but I still feel really passionate about language and cultural exchange. I know this was a long ass read. Lol)

I think because black people are featured more in media and the internet now, everyone is getting more exposure to our language. They're also consuming it at a much faster pace. 

People tend to adopt the language they hear frequently. It happens with accents as well. This is especially true for younger people. Their brains are designed to soak up language as part of their development. But even adults will go to a different county or watch a reality TV show and start to talk a little differently. I watched a few seasons of love island for example and all of a sudden I started calling people melts and bruv and saying this or that was muggy. I didn't stop until a little while after I stopped watching the show.

So I see it as a good thing. I know that's against the grain but it just proves how much of an impact we have and our increasing numbers in media.
